analysis.one_liner: Pays radiation victims of nuclear testing and uranium mining $150,000 and extends the compensation fund.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to expand compensation for radiation-exposed downwinders and uranium workers was introduced with 16 Senate cosponsors, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would reopen and expand the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act, the federal program that pays people whose health was harmed by nuclear weapons testing and uranium mining. It would add downwind communities the program never covered — including New Mexicans exposed to the Trinity test and residents of Guam — raise compensation to $150,000, extend uranium worker eligibility through 1990, cover kidney disease and new categories of workers like core drillers and ore transporters, add medical benefits, ease proof requirements (including accepting tribal records), and let previously denied or compensated claimants come back for new consideration. It would also extend the program's fund 19 years.
analysis.who_benefits: People with cancers and other radiation-linked illnesses who lived downwind of nuclear weapons tests in New Mexico, Nevada, Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Utah and Guam, and former uranium miners, millers, core drillers, ore transporters, and mine remediation workers (and their families) in western states, many of them on the Navajo Nation. People whose claims were previously denied could resubmit, and people already compensated could receive the difference if the new law pays more.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwinders and uranium workers with radiation illnesses

how_it_helps.text: Raises the standard compensation award for downwinders with covered cancers and diseases from $50,000 or $75,000 to a uniform $150,000, and adds chronic lymphocytic leukemia as a covered disease.
Adds New Mexico's Trinity test downwinders and Guam residents to the program for the first time, and stretches the covered physical-presence window for atmospheric tests out to November 6, 1962.

Extends uranium worker eligibility from mines and mills operating through 1971 to those operating through 1990, and adds kidney disease, core drillers, millers, ore transporters, remediation workers, and combined work histories to the covered categories.
Gives compensated claimants medical benefits on the same terms as Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program participants.

Lets claimants prove employment, residence, or test-site presence with sworn affidavits and, for tribal members, with grazing permits, homesite leases, post office box records, or letters from tribal leaders — proof that paper records often cannot supply.
Allows previously denied claimants to resubmit their claims up to three times, and pays people already compensated the difference if the amended law would have paid them more.
Extends the life of the Compensation Fund from 2 to 19 more years and extends the claims filing deadline accordingly.
Authorizes $3 million a year for university and nonprofit research on how uranium mining and milling affected non-workers, including miners' family members.

Adds uranium mine and mill workers to the Special Exposure Cohort pathway of the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program, which compensates workers whose exact radiation dose cannot be reconstructed.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the Radiation Exposure Compensation Fund and the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program. The uranium companies whose mines and mills made workers sick are not required to contribute anything; the government pays the claims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers through the compensation fund

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no offset for its costs: it extends the fund for 19 years, triples the standard award, adds whole new groups of claimants (Trinity downwinders, Guam residents, post-1971 uranium workers), pays top-ups to past recipients, and lets denied claimants try again up to three times, all without an estimate in the bill text of the total price to the Treasury.

The expanded evidence rules — sworn affidavits from a second person attesting to employment, residence, or test-site presence — make it easier to substantiate decades-old claims, which claimants' advocates consider essential but which weakens the documentary record behind each award; the bill does require the affidavits be under penalty of perjury and in addition to other evidence.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real, documented harm: the federal government detonated nuclear weapons upwind of communities and fueled its weapons program with uranium mined under conditions that sickened workers, and the existing program covered only part of that harm for only part of the affected areas. The honest cost is that all of it — an estimated tens of thousands of potential claims at $150,000 each, plus medical benefits and research — falls on the federal Treasury with no industry contribution and no offset, and the affidavit provisions invite some claims based on thin documentation. The scale of the public cost is real but bounded by the 19-year fund life.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico introduced the bill on May 18, 2023 with 16 original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Mike Crapo and Jim Risch of Idaho.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was ever listed on the bill: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House action occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal government kept the Radiation Exposure Compensation Fund closed to the newly covered groups — New Mexico Trinity downwinders, Guam residents, and post-1971 uranium workers — and the uranium industry kept an arrangement in which illnesses its operations caused are not charged against it. The sick workers and families the bill would have paid received nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal fund stayed closed; uranium industry kept its liability shield

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to expand compensation to New Mexico's Trinity-test downwinders and uranium workers and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 2 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.role: Senate Republican cosponsors (Sens. Crapo and Risch of Idaho)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan from the day of introduction.

against.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup during the two years it sat on the committee's docket.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — 16 cosponsors spanning 13 of 48 Senate Democrats, 2 of 49 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 4 Independents — and no one ever voted against it, because the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill pays for the illnesses of former uranium miners, millers, and transporters entirely from a federal fund; the companies that employed them contribute nothing. Letting the bill die kept that arrangement intact, with the public rather than the industry bearing the cost of its workforce's injuries.

industries.industry: Nuclear weapons complex (Department of Energy and its contractors)
industries.note: The bill routes uranium mine and mill workers into the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program, which would add claims and liability to a program administered for the DOE complex, while compensating people harmed by that complex's operations.
